desc:
In one operation you may pick two nodes that are on the same level of the tree and swap their values (the shape of the tree never changes). Return the minimum total number of operations needed so that on every level the values, read from left to right, are in strictly increasing order.

All node values of the tree are distinct, so the order inside a level is well defined. The empty tree needs 0 operations.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 4, 3, 7, 6, 8, 5, -1, -1, -1, -1, 9, -1, 10] the levels are [1], [4, 3], [7, 6, 8, 5] and [9, 10]. They need 0, 1, 2 and 0 swaps, so the answer is 3.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Swaps never move a value to another level, so every level can be solved on its own and the answers added.
For one level, compare the current order with the sorted order. Every value has a target position; follow value → target position → the value that sits there → and so on.
These chains form cycles. A cycle of length c can be fixed with exactly c - 1 swaps, and no fewer. So the cost of a level is its length minus its number of cycles.
editorial: Different levels are independent: a swap on one level never helps another. For a single level with values a[0..m-1], sort the indices by value to get the target position of each element. This defines a permutation, which splits into disjoint cycles. A cycle of length 1 is already in place; a cycle of length c > 1 needs c - 1 swaps (each swap can put at most one extra element in its final place, and the last swap fixes two). Hence the minimum number of swaps for the level is m - (number of cycles).
Computing the levels takes O(n), and sorting each level costs O(m log m), so the whole solution is O(n log n). Distinct values are what make the target positions unique.
